title: Using pERK immunostaining to quantify neuronal activity induced by stress in zebrafish larvae
protocol: Transfer 20 to 25 larvae to a new Petri dish (60 mm diameter) using a 3 mL plastic pipette approximately 75 minutes prior to the experiment.
Gently tilt the Petri dish and remove as much Danieau’s medium as possible.
Rapidly fill the Petri dish with 13 ml of fresh Danieau’s medium.
Leave the Petri dish containing zebrafish larvae at room temperature under light conditions for 60 minutes before the experiment.
Add 15 mL of Danieau’s solution to one Petri dish (control group).
Add 15 mL of 200 mM NaCl in Danieau's medium to another Petri dish (stressed group).
Distribute the solutions evenly across each Petri dish without swirling.
After 10 minutes, add 1.3 ml of tricaine to each Petri dish.
Rapidly transfer larvae from each Petri dish into separate microcentrifuge tubes.
Remove all solution inside the microcentrifuge tubes and replace with 1 mL of 4% PFA/PBT.
Handle PFA under a chemical hood and using personal protective equipment.
Fix the larvae for ∼18 h at 4°C placing the 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes horizontally without agitation.
Remove the PFA and wash the larvae three times with 1 mL of 1× PBT for 15 min at room temperature under agitation.
Handle PFA using personal protective equipment.
Discard liquid waste containing PFA under a chemical hood according to workplace safety instructions.
Incubate larvae with 500 μL of a clearing solution (3% H2O2 + 0.5% KOH in PBT) for 15 min at room temperature (∼23°C) with agitation (300 rpm).
Remove the clearing solution carefully, avoiding bubbles.
Rinse larvae with 1 mL of 1× PBS.
Wash larvae three times with 1 mL of 1× PBT under agitation for 15 minutes each time.
Store samples at 4°C for up to four days or at -20°C in MeOH for long-term storage.
Dehydrate larvae with 25% MeOH / 75% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation at room temperature.
Continue dehydrating with 50% MeOH / 50% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation.
Proceed to dehydrate with 75% MeOH / 25% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation.
Complete dehydration with 100% MeOH for 15 minutes.
Replace with fresh 100% MeOH and store larvae at -20°C.
Rehydrate larvae with 75% MeOH / 25% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation.
Continue rehydration with 50% MeOH / 50% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation.
Proceed to rehydrate with 25% MeOH / 75% PBT for 5 minutes under agitation.
Complete rehydration with 100% PBT for 5 minutes (repeat three times).
Use a 3 mL plastic pipette with a 10 μL tip to perform the washes.
Insert 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes into a 50 mL Falcon tube on a rotator.
Incubate larvae in 500 μL of 150 mM Tris-HCl in PBT for 5 minutes at room temperature without agitation.
Transfer the tubes containing larvae to a thermoblock set at 70°C and incubate for 15 minutes without agitation.
Remove the solution from the larvae.
Wash the larvae under agitation three times with 1 mL of 1× PBT for 15 minutes each wash.
Incubate the larvae in Trypsin-EDTA (diluted 1:50 in PBT) for 40 minutes on ice without agitation.
Remove the solution from the larvae.
Wash the larvae under agitation three times with 1 mL of 1× PBT for 15 minutes each wash.
Incubate the larvae in 700 μL of blocking solution for one hour at room temperature under agitation.
Incubate larvae overnight (12–16 h) at 4°C under agitation.
Dilute antibodies in 1,400 μL of blocking solution for two experimental groups.
Remove the blocking solution and replace with primary antibody solution (700 μl per tube).
Incubate larvae for 96 hours at 4°C with agitation.
Wash larvae three times with 1 mL of 1× PBT for 15 minutes at room temperature.
Increase the number of washes to remove excess primary antibody to reduce background.
Dilute antibodies in 1,400 μL of blocking solution for two tubes.
Remove PBT and replace with secondary antibody solution (700 μL per tube).
Incubate larvae for 48 h at 4°C under agitation.
Cover microcentrifuge tubes with aluminum foil to protect from light during preparation.
Wash larvae under agitation with 1 mL of 1× PBT three times for 15 min each.
Confirm antibody signal detectability using a fluorescence microscope.
Store larvae in the dark at 4°C up to three days if necessary.
Mount zebrafish larvae in low-melting-point agarose for confocal microscopy imaging.
Keep 1.5% low-melting-point agarose at 50°C during mounting to avoid solidification.
Place the mounted samples on the lid of a 35 mm plastic Petri dish for imaging.
Transfer a larva to the Petri dish’s lid using a plastic pipette.
Remove as much PBT as possible from around the larva.
Add one drop of agarose on top of the larva using a glass Pasteur pipette.
Gently orient the larva with its dorsal part up using a 10 μL pipette tip to expose the brain for imaging.
Repeat the process for all larvae intended for imaging, alternating samples belonging to different treatment conditions.
Once the agarose surrounding the larvae is solidified, add more agarose to connect the wall of the Petri dish’s lid to the larvae.
Orient the larvae as quickly as possible before the agarose solidifies.
Avoid touching the head while mounting the larvae.
Add minimal agarose to embed the larvae without disrupting the tissue.
Alternate larvae belonging to different treatment groups during mounting.
Cover the Petri dish’s lid containing the samples with PBS if using a water immersion objective.
Switch on the computer.
Switch on the microscope.
Switch on the fluorescent lamp.
Launch the microscope software (Zen Black).
Switch on the lasers to warm up.
Place the Petri dish containing the larvae on the microscope stage.
Press “Acquisition” in the Zen Black main window.
Select “Smart Setup” for automatic laser, light, path, and filter selection.
Choose dyes and pseudocolors in the Smart Setup window.
Choose "Smartest" acquisition mode.
Double-check detection range and laser for each fluorophore under “Imaging setup”.
Move the “Position” window to the center of the screen.
Locate the first mounted zebrafish larva and focus on the brain.
Press “Add” in the “Position” window.
Repeat steps a and b for all samples.
Save the position list.
Use "Move to" function to automatically move the microscope stage to each larva.
Save the positions of all samples to reduce adjustment time for imaging settings.
Press the "Acquisition" tab after using the "Smart Setup" function.
Press "Live" and focus on the area of interest.
Adjust settings by pressing “Channels”.
Set a “Laser Power” sufficient to observe fluorescent signals but as low as possible.
Use the ‘Range Indicator’ to set “Gain (Master)” while visualizing saturation.
Do not change “Digital Offset” and “Digital Gain”.
Set the "Pinhole Diameter" at 1 AU (Airy Unit).
Repeat all previous steps for each channel.
Move the stage using the "Move to" function in the "Position" window.
Verify that the fluorescence signal is below saturation in each fish.
Lower the “Gain” and/or the “Laser power” if the fluorescence signal is saturated in any region of interest.
Select “Frame” in the “Scan Mode” menu.
Choose 1024 × 1024 in the “Frame Size”.
Set the speed to a minimum of 8 for high scan speed.
Choose "Averaging" in the Acquisition Mode window to acquire multiple scans for noise reduction.
Select two scans to be acquired for each plane for sufficient noise reduction.
Under Method, choose the "Mean" option to average pixels from multiple scans.
Select 16 under Bit Depth for performing quantification of fluorescent signals.
Choose “Unidirectional” as the direction of the scan.
Move the stage to the first larva to be imaged and select the Z-stack option.
Focus on the top border of your region of interest and click "Set Last".
Move the focus until you reach the bottom of your region of interest and click "Set First".
Click “Optimal” to automatically set the slice number based on selected parameters.
Alternatively, manually set the parameters for the Z-stack.
Go to the Position window and select “Update”.
Open a multichannel image with ImageJ/Fiji.
Zoom on the neurons you intend to analyze.
Click on “Analyze”→ “Tools” → “ROI manager” to open the ROI window.
Select the first neuron you intend to analyze.
Set the ROIs for the measurement of the fluorescence intensity for each neuron.
Move the stack to the most ventral plane where your neuron of interest is visible.
Draw the region of interest over the outline of the neuron using the “Polygon selections” tool.
Use the channel with GFP labeling to identify the neuronal population of interest.
Click “Add” in the ROI window after drawing the ROI.
Repeat the operation for each plane where the neuron is visible.
Save the ROIs by clicking “More”→ “Save” in the ROI manager window.
Measure the fluorescence intensity of each channel in the selected ROIs.
Click “Analyze” → “Set measurements” and select “Integrated density.”
Select one of the channels, such as pERK, for measurement.
Select all the ROIs labeling your neuron of interest in the ROI window.
Click “Measure” in the ROI window to measure fluorescence intensity.
Repeat steps c and d for another channel, such as tERK.
Repeat steps 45 and 46 for all neurons of interest.
Copy-paste the measurements into a data-processing software like Excel, Python, or R.
Calculate the pERK/tERK ratios using your preferred data-processing software.
Sum the pERK Integrated Densities values for each plane of your neuron of interest.
Repeat the operation for every neuron.
Repeat steps a and b for the tERK channel.
For each neuron, calculate the ratio between the sums of pERK and tERK Integrated Densities values.
Plot your data to compare pERK/tERK values between stressed and not-stressed groups.
Perform statistical analyses to compare pERK/tERK values between stressed and not-stressed groups.
